---
title: "Nanoplots"
subtitle: "In-cell plots, drawn natively and scaled against one domain."
description: "format-nanoplot and the three renderers Keisen ships: nanoplot-line, nanoplot-points, and nanoplot-bar."
---

A nanoplot cell holds an array of readings, and [`format-nanoplot`](formatters.qmd) draws it through the function given as `plot`.
The domain spans every reading in the column, taken from the column itself, so the cells can be compared; that is the whole point, since sparklines scaled per cell say nothing.
`domain: (low, high)` overrides it for a column read against a scale that is not its own.

Three renderers ship, each drawn with native Typst primitives and each usable as `plot`.

| Function | Notable arguments |
| --- | --- |
| `nanoplot-line(numbers, ..)` | `domain: none`, `width: 4em`, `height: 0.8em`, `stroke: auto`, `thickness: 0.6pt`. A sparkline. |
| `nanoplot-points(numbers, ..)` | The same, plus `radius: 1pt`. A sparkline with its readings marked. |
| `nanoplot-bar(numbers, ..)` | `domain: none`, `width: 4em`, `height: 0.8em`, `fill: auto`, `gap: 30%`. Bars, measured from zero. |

: Nanoplot renderers {.striped .hover tbl-colwidths="[35,65]"}

`stroke: auto` and `fill: auto` follow the surrounding text colour, so a plot in a styled cell is drawn in that cell's ink.
Bars are measured from zero rather than from the domain's low, because a bar drawn from 5 to 10 makes a small difference look like the whole quantity; the line renderers scale to the domain instead, since a trend is about shape rather than magnitude.

A renderer is any `(numbers, domain: none, width: .., height: ..) => content`, so one written in a document works exactly as well as these.
